Fastest Token in the Town
Date: 2026-05-19
Status: Draft (as of 2026-05-21)
Jensen Huang famously declared that there is an insatiable demand for compute, and reoriented the whole company to satiate the insatiable demand, which now, 30 years later, is the most valuable company in the world.
Today on Tuesday May 19th, 2026. I, Harsh Gupta, declare that we theoric.com will produce the fastest token in town. Why, because like compute, there is an insatiable demand for speed.
The title is contested. We intend to earn it, defend it, and re-earn it every week.
Aim of this document
This document is the operating system for the current leg of Theoric.
It exists to:
Establish a sharp positioning that aligns the company so market forces can scale it.
Settle, in advance, the questions of what we sell, who we sell it to, and how we sell it.
Serve as a quick-reference artifact for day-to-day and hour-to-hour decisions, so we don't have to relitigate the strategy each time.
The document creates force. It says no on our behalf. It narrows attention. That is the mechanism, not a bug.
Non goals
This document is not:
The technical and engineering plan. That lives elsewhere.
A complete market analysis or go-to-market sequencing plan.
A philosophical statement about Theoric in general. The deeper worldview lives in Every problem is a software problem and in private founder doctrine.
Philosophy
The philosophy of this leg is single-pointed commitment to one finite game.
We commit to it fully. Not 99% with a 1% reserve. Not as a stepping stone with an exit ramp. Not with a caveat in the memo. The commitment is total because the problem is dense enough that total commitment to it is the right move on the merits.
The trust under the commitment is grounded in the structure of the problem, not in willpower or wishful thinking. Producing the fastest correct token, taken seriously, requires modeling hardware, workloads, memory, scheduling, correctness, cost, power, compilation, distributed execution, search itself, and agents that improve the system. That stack of modeling capabilities is large enough that depth in it produces capability beyond the surface problem.
A shallow trap just traps you. A deep trap becomes a tunnel.
This is the bet. Not that any total commitment opens into something larger, but that this specific commitment does, because going deep on this specific problem necessarily builds the modeling machinery that exceeds it. The depth is the mechanism. The commitment is the precondition for the depth.
Our operating principle, scoped to business problems on this leg: we engage with problems we can predictably solve as software problems with current capabilities, and where the engagement strengthens the modeling machinery itself. Problems outside that frame are not problems we take on as commercial work. We do not engage with chance-dependent bets disguised as ambition.
Speed is the position. Modeling is the practice. The capability is the asset.
How we got here
This position is sharper than where Theoric started, and the sharpening is the result of prior phases that have done their work.
The path: Autonomous AI Engineering as the original frame. GPU programming as the domain it grounded in, under the name Clockworks Compute. The discovery, while working on GPU programming, that formal methods plus AI agents had an unexpected fit,  agents handle the verbosity and proof burden that made Lean 4 impractical for humans, turning a theoretical advantage into a practical one. The Applied AI Lab framing that gave that insight room to develop beyond the original GPU programming frame. And now this contraction back to a sharper position than Clockworks Compute itself, informed by everything the Lab phase produced.
Each contraction has been narrower than the previous. Each phase between contractions has been deeper. The Lab phase looked from the outside like breadth; it was actually the breathing phase that produced the insight this contraction is built on. Fastest Token in Town is the application of that accumulated capability to a specific finite game, with the modeling depth that makes the commitment defensible.
What does it mean to be the fastest token in the town?
For any given workload, on a given hardware setup, the fastest token flows through us.
The qualifiers matter. We are not claiming we beat everyone on every configuration. We are claiming that for a declared model, workload, quality envelope, and hardware setup, we will be the fastest, and we will be able to demonstrate it.
The configuration space includes:
Model config: weights, quantization, adapters, context length, sampling
Workload config: prompt and output length distribution, concurrency, streaming, SLOs (TTFT, TPOT, p99)
Hardware config: host, device, count, topology, power cap
For any point or region in that space that a customer cares about, the title is contested. We earn it by being demonstrably faster on that configuration. We defend it by staying faster as the configuration evolves.
How will we do it?
We convert the problem of finding the fastest way to produce tokens, on a given workload and hardware, into an algorithmic search problem. We model the hardware, the workload, and the data mathematically. We search the execution space. We prove what can be proved, and benchmark what must be measured. We can demonstrate we are the fastest, with the evidence to back it.
What is in scope:
Anything that increases speed without compromising the declared quality envelope: speculative decoding, KV cache strategies, megakernels, disaggregated inference, removing host overhead.
Producing equivalent quality faster on different hardware: NVIDIA, AMD, TPU, Trainium, MatX, Cerebras, Tenstorrent. If anyone can produce faster tokens on a given hardware while keeping quality constant, we want to be part of that story.
Pareto-optimal positioning on the latency-throughput frontier.
Given a quantization level, given a power configuration, given a concurrency level, being the fastest at that point.
What might look out of scope but is in scope, because it is the same modeling problem under a different label:
Hardware design questions, where modeling lets us find faster chip layouts for inference workloads.
Memory design.
Better matmul techniques and algorithms.
New datatypes and quantization schemes for weights and KV cache.
Better ways to store and access KV cache.
The principle: if it makes our model of hardware-and-workload more accurate, more complete, or more usefully searchable, it is in scope. If it improves outcomes through means external to that model, it is not.
What is not in scope:
Cost optimization through procurement, contract negotiation, or finding cheaper GPU contracts.
Owning the GPU fleet. We do not want the financial liability of hardware.
Selling tokens directly to end customers. We do not want the distribution game.
Any other path to winning the inference game that doesn't route through making the fastest token.
The aim is the fastest token in town. The optimization pressure stays pointed at speed. If there are other ways to win the inference game, we do not go for them.
How will we make money?
We will not sell tokens directly. We will license our technology to whoever wants to produce the fastest token. The customer can sell the tokens externally, use them internally, set their own pricing, choose their own distribution method.
If they sell tokens externally, we take a tax (around 15%) on per-token pricing, or a cut of subscription revenue if they sell on subscription.
If they use tokens internally, we take a percentage of the hourly GPU pricing used to produce those tokens.
Enforcement is initially through contracts and lightweight telemetry built into the technology. Not every customer will accept this initially, and that is fine. The customers who care most about speed are the ones for whom the gap we provide is worth paying for, and they are the ones who will accept the terms. As the speed gap grows and our position becomes harder to substitute, the terms become easier to hold.
If a customer refuses the metering terms, the speed we are providing is not valuable enough to them. That is not a failed deal. That is the filter working.
Why does this business model make sense?
The business model is a forcing function, not a revenue strategy. Its purpose is to design the right optimization pressures and feedback loops so that we are the fastest, remain the fastest, and keep becoming faster.
If we are not meaningfully faster, the customer does not pay the tax. If speed is not what the customer cares about, the customer does not pay the tax. We are only rewarded for the dimension we have chosen to compete on. Everything else is structurally orthogonal to our revenue.
We have designed a company with no shock absorbers, and the design is deliberate. Shock absorbers don't just protect you from failure, they also dampen the signal from the market. The market is what propels us. Every layer of insulation we'd add, owning GPUs, selling tokens directly, building our own distribution, negotiating cloud contracts, is a layer that dampens that signal. We are stripping the insulation off so the coupling is direct. Not bravery. Transmission efficiency.
Each thing we are not doing is a thing that would have made us a different and worse company. The constraints are load-bearing. They are what keeps the optimization pressure pointed at speed.
If the customer cares about the fastest token, they will find us. For them to care, we need to be not just fast, but dramatically faster than the alternatives. The business model demands the technical position be real, and the technical position is what makes the business model viable. The two reinforce each other.
What this means day to day
If a task does not make the token faster, sharpen the measurement, shorten the loop, or strengthen the modeling and machinery that produces faster tokens, it is not the task.
If a customer wants something other than speed, they are not our customer right now.
If a technical bet does not have a predictable path to capability, we do not take it. Real opportunities without clear paths are inventory, not active work. They wait until current capabilities turn them from path-less to path-having. The current depth practice is also the most efficient way to unlock that inventory, depth in a sufficiently rich problem builds capabilities that travel.
If a competitor wins on a dimension we have chosen not to compete on, that is the design working. We do not chase them onto their ground.
The title is contested. We intend to earn it, defend it, and re-earn it every week.
Fastest Token in Town.
We can use the analogy to the Bezo’s framing, “people would always want their tokens to be faster and cheaper, as long as it is the same token”

content.text:
**Foreign qualification** means registering your Delaware corporation to do business in another state (e.g. California if you’re operating from SF).

Delaware is where the company is *incorporated*. If you have a real presence elsewhere — office, employees, regular business — that other state often wants you registered as a “foreign” (out-of-state) corporation there. It’s a separate state filing + fees; Clerky’s Lifetime package doesn’t include those third-party costs.

Whether you need it soon depends on where you’re actually operating and that state’s rules; many early startups incorporate in DE first and handle foreign qual when they clearly have nexus in another state.

content.text:
Yes Dropping Demis, I have lot more functional needs around learning. What else is remaining to define this project properly?

BTW, I do think I need some readings on project management, put "learn how to do project management well" at the bottom of the projects list.

--- ---

About ALV3 strengthening: it depends on strong project definitions. If we define software requirements well, we can use ALV3 to get those projects done. The current agents are also generally good, so we might not need it. Success criteria are unclear because we don’t know when they will be done. If ALV3 is successful, we will have strong guarantees and confidence in the outcome, and the process can be defined per project. ALV3’s characteristics include explicit context and explicit actions, providing more confidence and visibility, and allowing composition.

If ALV3 is done well, we will see several advantages over other agents. We may also use ALV3 in project‑requirement agents, but that is deferred. Success for ALV3 means better performance on appropriate benchmarks, which we must create to define good success criteria. The downstream project is evals; this is the upstream eval for ALV3.

Failure scenarios: a good failure is poor performance on the benchmarks. A bad failure is a murky situation where we cannot tell if it is performing well, and we lack clarity on what is correct. Actual failures would look like spending four to six sessions on it without knowing how to proceed, which would be a major failure. 

--- ---

"proj-requirements-agents"

Okay, I will split this into two parts. For each item, we should add why it is relevant; that will define what success looks like. We also need to specify what happens on success, which I haven’t mentioned yet but is implicit in the motivations. If anything is unclear, just ask me.

For the project requirements agent, there are three parts:

1. Can we formally specify requirements so that we can unambiguously determine whether the project was done well? Agents often claim they are finished, but they may have missed something that looks like success. We need clear criteria to confirm completion.

2. Can we make agents follow those formal specifications?

3. Given the formal requirements, can we ensure agents fulfill them?

If we do this well, we will have software that we can clone with high confidence and reliability, and we can ship it to the customer confidently. 

Failure is defined as not being able to capture the requirements properly, or not knowing whether we have captured them successfully. This makes verification and validation much more difficult, time‑consuming, and increases the need for customer involvement. 

Success means we can differentiate between requirements that are properly defined and those that are not, allowing us to identify which software is ready for deployment and which is not. Failure, conversely, means we cannot make that distinction, leading to higher costs in time, effort, and human resources.

content.text:
Insights:
- Each person has it's own style
- Elon focuses a lot on relevance. You should very very clearly establish relevance first, and this also reflects in his management style "best requirement is no requirement"
- Gates is a Grinder, he focuses on absorbing a lot of information, making sure he retains it by taking notes, and mentally debating with the author. To make sure he understands the material well
- Justin Skycak focuses a lot on skill based learning, skill tree. Skill based learning is different from "just knowing" something. A skill should allow you to do something which you could not do before, and ideally in a reliable and consistent manner.


Observations from on my methods, and general recommendations:
- I prefer YT, and podcasts, as opposed to physical books
- Take a LOT of voice notes.
- And Like to walk or drive scooter while listening/thinking
- Don't have an established practice of establishing explicit relevance, or establishing explicitly what skills am I looking to gain.

Recommendation:
- Try to establish relevance, you do very little of it, partly probably you *like* to absorb information. But try to be deliberate about it, for every hour spent on trying to learn something, spend 5-10 minutes establishing relevance. What are the ways this specific information I'm about to consume, how will it help me. In what scenarios. Later you can develop the skill of dropping learning projects which aren't directly relevant, and/or rescoping them to be lot more effective.
- Try to recap the core points of what you learn, why does the author/speak belive it to be true, what the cases it might not be true.
- Related to the relevance point, try to be explicit about what skill does this learning project give me, and know if it is an awareness project, or a skill project, sometimes just being aware of existance of a certain thing is also useful, and sometimes it is entertaining to absorb a certain peice of information, entertainment is not bad, but explicit. For skill based project, try to what does the relevant skill look like.

content.text:
Hand writing:

Everything I know about requirements engineering:
- It _is_ possible to specify the requirements of the software, and prove that if the conditions are satisfied, the software works well, and correctly. Classic Example: Sorting function, the output type can be specified as a sorted permutation of the input list, and your compiler will catch the bugs. I know how to do that with function signatures for small mathematical functions. Here the function signature is validated by human, and assumed to be true.
- It _is_ possible to 1. formally capture the requirements, 2. in a way which allows you to prove the requiements themselves to be well formed. And 3. Those requirements then can be used to prove the correctness, and/or completeness of your software.
- Rewriting a piece of software in Lean does not magically make it fast or correct.

Everything I know about using LLMs to create software well:
- Honestly, I don't know how to use LLMs to create software well. I prompt and does things, then I check things it did, often it does the right thing, but sometimes it forgets or miss stuff, or has a subtle bug.
- It is decent at following textual specifications, and you can ask it checkbox everything, and grind till all the boxes are filled, and it does the job, and yet it will be cheating in some ways.
- The only current way which seems to work, is have a good and strong definition of work, make llm do the thing, test everything, check everything, give feedback, and repeat. It reduces, removes a lot of bugs, and often you can get a place where you have something working somewhat well to be useful, often that "something" can be a fairly big pieces, which might have taken you months pre-llms. So the size of the pieces you are able to hand off has been growing, and confidence is growing. But it is more "trust" than confidence, as in similar to way you trust a backend engineer will be able to make a API service, and frontend a UI, and they won't make "basic" mistakes, correct in that way.

Learning Goals:
- Develop the skill of being able to specify software requirements well

  - id: proj-requirements-agents
    name: Formal requirements capture → drive agents
    cluster: solutioning_method
    one_liner: >
      Formally specify requirements so completion is unambiguous, make agents
      follow those specs, and ensure they fulfill them — then ship with confidence.
    why_relevant: >
      Agents often claim finished when something was missed that looks like
      success. Without formal requirements we cannot tell done from faux-done;
      V&V gets harder, slower, more customer-heavy. Success here lets us know
      which software is deploy-ready.
    refs:
      - jackson_book: "Software Requirements & Specifications (Michael Jackson)"
      - blocks: [req-jackson-1, req-jackson-2, req-synth, req-apply, req-capture-invest-1]
    parts:
      - id: part-specify
        name: Formally specify requirements
        why_relevant: >
          So we can unambiguously determine whether the project was done well.
          Agents claim finished; we need clear criteria to confirm completion.
          Also load-bearing for long vision: specify what correct software looks like.
        question: Can we formally specify requirements so done is unambiguous?
        learning_goal: Develop the skill of specifying software requirements well
        known_so_far:
          - Spec + prove-if-conditions → works (e.g. sorted permutation); small math fn signatures
          - Formal capture + prove requirements well-formed + use for correctness/completeness is possible
          - Lean rewrite ≠ magically fast or correct
      - id: part-follow
        name: Make agents follow the formal specifications
        why_relevant: Specs that agents ignore do not change outcomes.
        question: Can we make agents follow those formal specifications?
        learning_goal: >
          Specify so we can mechanistically check correctness/completeness of the
          spec; enable fully autonomous unsupervised implementation on normal
          harnesses; unlock stronger harnesses (OOM faster / fewer tokens / ≥ quality)
          by formalizing software creation itself.
        good_looks_like: >
          Very high human confidence software works; unspecified cases covered or
          known; requirement bugs/mismatches surfaced early; limitations known;
          software well behaved.
        next_practice:
          - Formally specify tic-tac-toe; observe what/how well
          - Then library management system; same observation
        roadmap_sketch:
          - Read Jackson — sense of specifying software well
          - Articulate formally specifiable vs not
          - List increasingly hard projects to specify/prove/build
          - Include regular apps (games, mobile, web) not only DB/OS/compilers
      - id: part-fulfill
        name: Ensure agents fulfill the requirements
        why_relevant: Following process ≠ meeting the actual requirements.
        question: Given formal requirements, can we ensure agents fulfill them?
        learning_goal: ""  # still open — or merge with part-follow.good_looks_like if user confirms
        known_so_far: "Current loop: define → LLM → test/check/feedback/repeat (trust > confidence)"
    scope: >

    success_criteria: >

      and which is not. On the happy path: software we can clone with high

{"contents":"# Compute v0.1 — Product Brief

The complete product contract is in [`spec.md`](spec.md); locked and open choices are in [`decisions.md`](decisions.md).

## Product

Compute by Theoric is serverless remote execution for Python GPU functions. A developer installs the `compute` package (**UF-01**), authenticates with `compute setup` (**UF-02**), adds prepaid credit (**UF-03**), and runs a function on a fresh cloud GPU with `compute run file.py::fn` or `.remote()` (**UF-05**). Logs and the JSON result come back (**UF-06**); billing, teardown, result transfer, and catalog/rate sync are internal (**IF-01**–**IF-04**). Flow definitions: [`launch_checklist.md`](launch_checklist.md). Status (working / not working): [`flows/README.md`](flows/README.md).

The default GPU is a 1× AMD MI300X from Hot Aisle. Supported 1× RunPod SKUs (datacenter and consumer, curated) use the same interface through the isolated deprecated REST v1 adapter. Providers are explicit in the catalog; v0.1 does not promise automatic failover.

## User and problem

The initial user is an independent ML engineer or small AI team that needs occasional high-memory GPU access but does not want to manage cloud accounts, drivers, images, SSH, provisioning, metering, or cleanup.

## Value proposition

- Easier than managing GPU infrastructure: no Dockerfiles, SSH, driver setup, or cloud-console lifecycle.
- Cost-transparent: prepaid per-minute provider pricing plus an itemized platform fee, a clearly labeled preflight estimate, and automatic termination.
- Reproducible: every run starts on a fresh machine with curated images and an AST-selected source payload.
- Familiar: a deliberately limited, silent source translator supports common Modal-shaped functions, without advertising compatibility or parity.

Lower cost than Modal is a hypothesis to validate with measured supported-workload comparisons, not an unqualified launch claim.

## v0.1 boundary

In scope: Python SDK/CLI, sync and detached runs, 1× GPUs, curated ROCm/CUDA images, dependency layers, secrets, logs, run history, cancellation, prepaid billing, and a dashboard.

Out of scope: idle or warm machines, SSH, multi-GPU, persistent volumes, HTTP endpoints, cron, queues, retries, custom Dockerfiles, teams, multi-region, reservations, and spot.

## Business and success

Payment is prepaid through Stripe under WOW21, Inc., with a $10 minimum top-up. Users pay the locked provider rate plus a marginal platform fee. The week-1 **internal target** is **$100 of prepaid credit consumed for provider usage plus platform fee by external accounts**; unused top-ups and internal accounts do not count. That target is a tracking metric, not a kill bar. Product source stays private (`theoriclabs/compute.cx`); public GitHub is marketing/docs/issues only.","totalLinesInFile":32}

{"contents":"# B4 — Fast follower (2026-08-09)

Started at Raavi while waiting for biryani (~15:45). Awareness session; not skill-building.

## Learning goal
Become **aware** of cases where companies successfully executed the **fast follower** technique well.

Single session ≈ awareness only. Real skill needs more passes.

## Relevance (compute.cx)
compute.cx is meant as Modal / Tinker alternatives — move their customers to us.

### Option 1 — Disruption / underserved
Find underserved customer / category / value prop and serve that.
Usually a somewhat different product or different positioning (classic disruption).

### Option 2 — Fast follower
New product is somewhat different, not a clone — but close enough to call FF.
Example: Claude (chat product, not Claude Code) is widely called a fast follower of ChatGPT.

**If we go Option 2 → need a clear picture of what “doing it well” looks like.**

This session targets Option 2 awareness.

{"contents":"
### F. Facebook vs MySpace / (later) Instagram copy dynamics
- Mixed; useful only as “same social graph job, better execution/trust/college wedge” — don’t overfit.

### G. Closer to compute.cx — cloud / infra FF vibes
- **AWS → others:** Azure/GCP as FF into “cloud IaaS/PaaS” after AWS educated market — win via enterprise relationships, hybrid, credits, specific workloads.
- **Heroku → Render/Fly/Railway etc.:** same “deploy app without ops” job; differentiation on DX, pricing, regions — classic FF into an educated segment.
- **Colab / notebook hosts → lots of followers:** category known; compete on GPUs, collab, pricing.
- **Modal / Replicate / together-style inference platforms:** market already taught “serverless GPU / run inference without owning fleet.” A Modal/Tinker alternative is naturally Option-2-shaped: **same buyer language, switch pitch, not inventing GPU cloud.**

## Implications for compute.cx (Option 2 hypothesis)
If Modal/Tinker already taught the segment:
- Spend less on “what is serverless GPU?” and more on **why switch** (price, reliability, DX, model/runtime fit, support, credits, region, AMD wedge, etc.).
- Product can differ (positioning, SKUs, runtime) and still be FF if customers put you in the **same consideration set**.
- “Doing it well” ≈ **credible parity on the jobs they already pay for** + **one sharp reason to move** + **low switching friction** — not a sci-fi new category story.

## Open questions for next passes
- [ ] Which Modal/Tinker jobs are non-negotiable for a switch vs nice-to-have?
- [ ] Historical FF cases: what was the *minimum* parity bar vs the wedge?
- [ ] Where does Option 1 (underserved wedge) beat pure Option 2 for us?
- [ ] Dump personal stories (Claude, Excel/Lotus, others) in “what I know” above before more research.
